extracted.intended_audience: scholars and students of media studies, sociology of news, and crime/media researchers
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating how newspapers select, frame, and sustain news about crime (specifically 'mugging') using news values, labels, authoritative sources, and packaging (headlines, photos, quotes). Useful for content-analysis and critical media studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty (primary news value)
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'news value' of 'novelty' — initial driver of newsworthiness for a new label/theme but with the most limited life span.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Novelty initially focuses attention (e.g. on female violence or 'mod'/'rocker' labels) but through repetition the extraordinary becomes ordinary; as novelty declines other news values are needed to sustain the story's 'news-life'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of supplementary or augmenting news values
rubrics_metrics.description: Supplementary news values (e.g., 'bizarre', 'violence', 'famous person') are used to revive or extend the life of a story once novelty wanes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors emphasise that these values operate as a structure or set around the primary value of novelty — different ways of reviving a 'waning' news story. In the mugging case, 'bizarre' and 'violence' in particular augmented declining newsworthiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bizarre / whimsical / unusual circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'bizarre' report is one with highly unusual, odd, eccentric, quaint, strange or grotesque characteristics; can be humorous or menacing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bizarre items subdivide into humorous twists or menacing/grotesque overtones; such items gain visibility by the oddity and can co-exist with 'violence' as supplementary news values. Example stories (e.g., 'Muggers pick on the wrong man') illustrate the humorous variety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Violence as a structuring news value
rubrics_metrics.description: The presence of violence (actual physical violence vs threat/no reported violence) increases news visibility and structures reportage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reports were coded as 'violent' when involving actual physical violence and 'non-violent' when only threat or no reported violence; the authors note growth in violent mugging reports and use ratios (violent:non-violent) to demonstrate intensification. They also caution about differences between reported descriptions and formal charges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seriousness of the event
rubrics_metrics.description: The perceived seriousness of the offence is an important selection factor for crime news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Roshier's factors are cited: seriousness was listed first among important criteria influencing selection of crime news; seriousness functions as part of the core newsworthiness assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Involvement of famous or high-status people
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'elite or famous person' news-value: the involvement of a famous/high-status person increases newsworthiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In this sample the 'elite or famous person' did not play a major augmenting role (only five stories gained visibility primarily because of a famous name), but it is identified as a classic news-value used elsewhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentimental or dramatic circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: Sentimental or dramatic circumstances (emotive or dramatic detail) increase newsworthiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited among Roshier's important factors; such circumstances help dramatise and moralise stories, making them more newsworthy and headline-worthy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Headline juxtaposition and contrast as an attention device
rubrics_metrics.description: Headlines often augment a story's news value by counterposing contrasting or oppositional themes (e.g., youth of offenders vs length of sentences).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Headlines dramatise events and indicate why an item is important; juxtaposition serves to signal problem/issue and to position the story within a broader pattern (e.g., '16-year-old' vs '20 years').

rubrics_metrics.name: Labeling / creative use of labels (e.g., 'mugging')
rubrics_metrics.description: The media's choice to label an event (e.g., calling a case 'mugging') is a creative definitional act that structures subsequent inference and debate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Labels may not be used in court but appear in headlines; using the 'mugging' label ensures the ensuing debate is 'inferentially structured' from the outset and aligns the story with an ongoing theme or moral panic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anchorage in authoritative pronouncements / use of privileged definers
rubrics_metrics.description: News stories are anchored in authoritative statements (judges, police, ministers) that justify or legitimate the coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The press often uses judges' or officials' remarks (e.g., 'Mugging is becoming more and more prevalent') to justify labels and headlines; such 'anchorage' gives media-defined categories external authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reciprocity between media and primary definers (mutual reinforcement)
rubrics_metrics.description: A reciprocal relationship exists where media deploy definitions from authorities, and authorities (courts, police, politicians) in turn use media/public opinion to legitimise actions — closing a circle of reinforcement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include courts using 'public opinion' (as reported by media) to justify sentencing and the media legitimising control policies by reporting judicial or police pronouncements; the authors term this interaction part of an 'amplification spiral' and argue the media can function as an 'ideological state-apparatus'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of statistics to justify or legitimate framing
rubrics_metrics.description: Quoting crime statistics (e.g., percentage increases) is used to legitimate particular framings or policy responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Papers recalled figures (like a claimed 129% rise in muggings) to implicitly justify harsh sentences and to move the issue from purely judicial to political framing; authors caution about problems with official statistics but note their rhetorical power in coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection and personalization of actors and images
rubrics_metrics.description: Choosing which actors to quote (offenders, families, experts, pressure groups) and which photographs to publish personalises and frames abstract issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Photographs of offenders and mothers, and quotations from family members, individualise the abstract themes (e.g., youth/innocence vs law) and can indicate a paper's stance (populist vs abstract). The presence/absence of mitigation pleas in some papers prefigured later emphases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Framing through choice of additional contextual material
rubrics_metrics.description: Editorial choices to include or omit parliamentary/ministerial statements, prior speeches, or comparative references (e.g., American mugging) frame the case politically and legally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Including political-legal statements can suggest government approval or situate a case within a larger law-and-order agenda; omitting mitigating information or pleas can prefigure punitive coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counting/inclusion rule for content analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Methodological rule: count all items mentioning the focal label ('mugging'), including case reports, general reports, features, and editorials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors note most items referred to particular cases but a substantial number were general pieces (Home Office activity, features, editorials) and that consistently these latter kinds provided about a quarter or more of all items — an explicit inclusion decision for content-analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliance on reported descriptions rather than formal charges
rubrics_metrics.description: In coding 'violence' the authors relied on reported descriptions in the press, not on formal charges brought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They acknowledge potential mismatches between press descriptions and official records, and this methodological choice affects classification (violent vs non-violent) and any ratio-based claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Difficulty distinguishing instrumental vs gratuitous violence in reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: News reporting may blur instrumental (goal-directed) violence and gratuitous (senseless) violence; headlines that emphasize 'violent' may belie more ambiguous motives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors note lack of precise quantitative evidence to separate 'purely gratuitous' from 'instrumental' violence but argue an overall increase in 'violent' reports matters as a structuring news value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Headlines' dual function: attention and problematisation
rubrics_metrics.description: Headlines must draw attention (dramatise) and indicate why the item is important/problematic — often by using sensational words ('shock', 'sensation').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beyond sensationalism, headlines indicate the problematic angle of a story (e.g., framing Handsworth as part of a 'mugging' pattern and as a question about penal policy) and thereby shape subsequent public debate.
